dictionaries.notes: Ten topics: taught by 8/8 courses (deep), and B06 handed over dict(zip()), tuple keys, sorting a dict by value and dict.copy(). Mapping patterns in match (deferred by B04) are in nested_data_structures.match_structure_patterns. Hash table internals are a later batch (hash_maps_internals). Generic hints like dict[str, int] were not given a KP; B09 tool_mypy or a stitching pass may add them. Storing functions as dict values (100 Days calculator) is B08 higher_order_functions. Reading word data from files into dicts is B10 file_io; json is B10.

sets.notes: Three core topics. Set comprehensions are dict_comprehensions.transform_dicts KP4. frozenset and the in-place operators (|=, &=) were left out (codecademy only). Big-O of set membership is a later algorithms batch.

nested_data_structures.notes: Grid topics own 2D lists; copying.shallow_vs_deep (B06, non-core) already teaches the [[0] * 3] * 3 trap and deepcopy, so it is not repeated; list_comprehensions.nested_comprehensions revisits safe grid building. match_structure_patterns adds the sequence patterns (B06 handoff) and mapping patterns (B04 handoff) in one non-core topic; it has no taught_in because none of the 8 courses teaches them. JSON parsing itself is B10 json_data, which should depend on navigate_deep_data. Recursion over nested lists/trees is B08 recursion.

list_comprehensions.notes: any()/all() and summing booleans (B05 handoff) are in any_all_and_sum. Its KP4 previews generator expressions only as 'brackets can go inside a call'; laziness, generator objects and yield are B08 generators, which should encompass any_all_and_sum. map()/filter() as alternatives are B08 higher_order_functions. Reconciliation: any_all_and_sum KP4 (dropping the brackets = generator expression preview) was removed; generators.generator_expressions (B08, the owner) now depends on any_all_and_sum.

dict_comprehensions.notes: Two topics; transform_dicts also owns set comprehensions.

stacks_queues.notes: Non-core (bootdev DSA and codecademy only). deque is taught here, so collections_module does not repeat it. Linked-list implementations are a later batch (linked_lists); recursion's call stack is B08.

collections_module.notes: Counter, defaultdict and namedtuple (B06 handoff); deque lives in stacks_queues.queue_with_deque. OrderedDict, ChainMap and UserDict/UserList were left out (plain dicts keep order since 3.7). 'from collections import X' is used as a memorised line before B13 modules_imports. dataclasses as the modern record type belong to the OOP batch (B11).

itertools_module.notes: Two non-core topics. zip(strict=True) (B06 handoff) is chain_count_zip_longest KP4. groupby, accumulate, islice and cycle were left out; generator pipelines are B08 generators.

knowledge_points.title: Dict literal and lookup by key
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed value for lookups in a 3-entry dict; write the lookup expression for a named key.

knowledge_points.title: Values of any type, len() and the empty dict
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() of dict literals; write a dict literal from a described table.

knowledge_points.title: Why a dict beats a list of pairs
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the structure that answers a lookup question in one expression; convert a short list of pairs to a dict literal.

knowledge_points.title: Missing keys raise KeyError
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each lookup prints a value or raises KeyError; fix a lookup with the wrong key case.

topics.title: Adding, updating and deleting entries
topics.summary: Mutate a dict: add a new key, overwrite or increment an existing one, delete with del and pop, and merge with update().

knowledge_points.title: Assigning to a new key adds it
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict after a sequence of assignments; write code that builds a described dict from empty.

knowledge_points.title: Assigning to an existing key overwrites it
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values after mixed add, overwrite and += steps; spot the += that fails on a missing key.

knowledge_points.title: Removing entries with del and pop
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict and the returned value; choose del, pop or pop with a default for described tasks.

knowledge_points.title: Merging another dict with update() and |
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the merged dict when keys overlap; fill in update or | for in-place vs new-dict tasks.

topics.title: Checking for keys with in and get()
topics.summary: Avoid KeyError by testing keys with in, or by reading with get() and a default value.

knowledge_points.title: in checks keys, not values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ages = {'ana': 31, 'bo': 27}
print('ana' in ages)  # True
print(31 in ages)     # False
Membership on a dict looks only at its keys.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict True/False for in tests on keys and values; multiple choice on what in searches.

knowledge_points.title: Check before you look up
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that crashes on a missing key; predict output for present and missing names.

knowledge_points.title: get() returns None for a missing key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ages = {'ana': 31, 'bo': 27}
print(ages.get('bo'))  # 27
print(ages.get('cy'))  # None
get never raises; it hands back None when the key is absent.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict get results; write an if that checks the result of get for None.

knowledge_points.title: get(key, default) supplies your own fallback
knowledge_points.practice: Predict get with defaults; multiple choice on whether get changed the dict.

topics.title: Looping over keys, values and items
topics.summary: Loop over a dict's keys, its values() and its items() with unpacking, and search a dict by value.

knowledge_points.title: A for loop over a dict gives its keys
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed lines; write a loop that prints every key with its value.

knowledge_points.title: values() when only the values matter
knowledge_points.practice: Write a total or maximum over values(); predict loop output over values().

knowledge_points.title: items() with unpacking
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of an items() loop; fix a loop that unpacks a plain dict loop into two names.

knowledge_points.title: Finding keys by value needs a loop
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop collecting all keys with a given value; predict output when no value matches.

topics.title: Counting occurrences with a dictionary
topics.summary: The histogram idiom: increment a per-key count with if/else or get(key, 0), count words in text, and find the most common key.

knowledge_points.title: Count with if/else
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of the counting loop; predict counts for a short string or list.

knowledge_points.title: Count with get(key, 0)
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite an if/else counter using get; fix a counter written as counts[ch] += 1 on an empty dict.

knowledge_points.title: Counting words in a line of text
knowledge_points.practice: Write a word counter for a sentence; predict counts when case differs.

knowledge_points.title: Find the most common key
knowledge_points.practice: Write a function returning the most frequent word; fix a version that compares keys instead of counts.

topics.title: Grouping values into lists by key
topics.summary: Build a dict whose values are lists (group words by first letter, invert a dict) with an if-not-in check or setdefault().

knowledge_points.title: Create the list the first time, then append
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the grouping loop; predict the groups for a short word list.

knowledge_points.title: The overwrite bug
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the line that loses earlier items; predict the buggy output.

knowledge_points.title: setdefault() does the check for you
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite an if-not-in grouping loop with setdefault; predict what setdefault returns.

knowledge_points.title: Inverting a dict: value to list of keys
knowledge_points.practice: Write an inversion for a given dict; predict the inverted result.

topics.title: Converting between dicts and pairs: dict(), zip() and items()
topics.summary: Build a dict from a list of pairs or from two lists with zip, turn a dict back into lists, and use a dict as a lookup table.

knowledge_points.title: dict() from a list of pairs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pairs = [('a', 1), ('b', 2)]
d = dict(pairs)
print(d)  # {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
Each 2-item tuple becomes one key-value entry.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict built from pairs (including a repeated key, where the last wins).

knowledge_points.title: dict(zip(keys, values)) from two lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['ana', 'bo']
ages = [31, 27]
print(dict(zip(names, ages)))  # {'ana': 31, 'bo': 27}
zip pairs the lists position by position; dict turns the pairs into entries.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the one-liner for two given lists; predict the result when the lists differ in length.

knowledge_points.title: Back to lists: list(d), values() and items()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
d = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
print(list(d))           # ['a', 'b']
print(list(d.values()))  # [1, 2]
print(list(d.items()))   # [('a', 1), ('b', 2)]
list() over a dict gives keys; wrap values() or items() to get the other views as lists.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict each conversion; fill in the call that produces a requested list.

knowledge_points.title: A dict as a lookup table instead of an elif chain
knowledge_points.worked_example:
day_names = {1: 'Mon', 2: 'Tue', 3: 'Wed'}
n = 2
print(day_names.get(n, 'unknown'))  # Tue
print(day_names.get(9, 'unknown'))  # unknown
One table plus get replaces a ladder of if n == 1 ... elif n == 2 ... else.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite an elif chain as a dict lookup; translate a word letter by letter with a given table.

topics.title: Sorting a dictionary by key or by value
topics.summary: Print a dict in key order, sort its items by value with flipped tuples or key=d.get, and report the top n.

knowledge_points.title: sorted() on a dict sorts its keys
knowledge_points.worked_example:
counts = {'b': 1, 'a': 3, 'c': 2}
print(sorted(counts))          # ['a', 'b', 'c']
print(sorted(counts.items()))  # [('a', 3), ('b', 1), ('c', 2)]
Both sort by key; the dict itself is unchanged.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict sorted() over a dict and over its items; write a loop that prints entries in key order.

knowledge_points.title: Sort by value: flip to (value, key)
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the flip-and-sort lines; predict the order including ties on value.

knowledge_points.title: key=d.get sorts keys by their values
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result; fix key=counts.get() called by mistake.

knowledge_points.title: Top n most common
knowledge_points.practice: Write a top-3 report from a counts dict; predict output for n larger than the dict.

topics.title: Which values can be keys: tuple keys
topics.summary: Know that keys must be immutable (a list key raises TypeError) and use tuples as keys for names and grid coordinates.

knowledge_points.title: Lists cannot be keys
knowledge_points.worked_example:
d = {}
d[(1, 2)] = 'ok'
d[[1, 2]] = 'no'  # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
Keys must be unchangeable values such as str, int and tuple; a list could change after being stored.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which assignments raise TypeError; fix a dict that uses a list as a key.

knowledge_points.title: Tuple keys for two-part names
knowledge_points.worked_example:
phone = {('Ana', 'Lee'): '555-1234'}
print(phone[('Ana', 'Lee')])  # 555-1234
print(phone['Ana', 'Lee'])    # 555-1234
The whole tuple is the key; the parentheses inside [ ] are optional.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a lookup with a tuple key; predict lookups with a partial key (KeyError).

knowledge_points.title: Coordinates as keys: a sparse grid
knowledge_points.worked_example:
board = {(0, 0): 'X', (1, 2): 'O'}
print(board.get((1, 2), '.'))  # O
print(board.get((2, 2), '.'))  # .
Store only the filled squares; get with a default fills in the rest.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict board lookups; write code placing a mark at a given row and column.

knowledge_points.title: Unpacking tuple keys in a loop
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the loop lines; fix a loop that unpacks into three names without parentheses.

topics.title: Dicts are mutable: aliasing, copying and changing while looping
topics.summary: Predict aliasing of dicts, copy one with copy(), see a function change the caller's dict, and avoid changing a dict's size while looping over it.

knowledge_points.title: Two names, one dict
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both dicts after changes through an alias.

knowledge_points.title: copy() makes an independent dict
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a backup that changes with the original; predict outputs with copy vs plain assignment.

knowledge_points.title: Functions can change the caller's dict
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the caller's dict after calls; choose between mutating and returning a new dict.

knowledge_points.title: Don't add or delete keys while looping over the dict
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a cleanup loop; predict which loops raise RuntimeError (adding/deleting keys vs updating values).

topics.title: Sets: unique values and fast membership
topics.summary: Create a set from a literal or a list to remove duplicates, test membership, and avoid the {} and indexing pitfalls.

knowledge_points.title: A set keeps each value once
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = {3, 1, 3, 2, 1}
print(len(s))       # 3
print(sorted(s))    # [1, 2, 3]
Duplicates are dropped; a set has no fixed order, so sort it when you need to display it in order.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() of set literals with repeats; predict sorted() of a set.

knowledge_points.title: set(list) removes duplicates
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['hi', 'yo', 'hi', 'hi']
print(len(set(words)))  # 2
print(sorted(set('banana')))  # ['a', 'b', 'n']
Converting to a set is the quick way to count or list the distinct values.
knowledge_points.practice: Write an expression counting distinct items; predict the distinct letters of a word.

knowledge_points.title: Empty set is set(), not {}
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type({}))     # <class 'dict'>
print(type(set()))  # <class 'set'>
print({'a'} == set('a'))  # True
{} is an empty dict; braces only make a set when they contain values.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that starts a set with {} and then calls add; multiple choice on the type of brace expressions.

knowledge_points.title: Membership yes, indexing no
knowledge_points.worked_example:
vowels = {'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u'}
print('e' in vowels)  # True
print(vowels[0])  # TypeError: 'set' object is not subscriptable
Sets answer 'is it in here?' quickly but have no positions.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict in tests and the indexing error; choose list or set for described tasks.

topics.title: Adding and removing set items
topics.summary: Grow a set with add(), remove items with remove() or discard(), and use a 'seen' set to find or drop duplicates.

knowledge_points.title: add() ignores values already present
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tags = set()
tags.add('red')
tags.add('blue')
tags.add('red')
print(len(tags))  # 2
Adding a duplicate is not an error; it just changes nothing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the size after a sequence of adds; write a loop adding every word of a list.

knowledge_points.title: remove() vs discard()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tags = {'red', 'blue'}
tags.discard('green')   # no error
tags.remove('green')    # KeyError: 'green'
remove insists the value is there; discard quietly does nothing if it is not.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which line errors; choose remove or discard for a described task.

knowledge_points.title: A 'seen' set finds repeats
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the seen-set loop; write a function returning True if a list has any duplicate.

knowledge_points.title: Remove duplicates but keep the order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
seen = set()
result = []
for x in [4, 7, 4, 1, 7]:
    if x not in seen:
        seen.add(x)
        result.append(x)
print(result)  # [4, 7, 1]
set(lst) loses the order; a seen set plus a result list keeps first appearances in order.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the order-preserving dedupe; fix a version that appends before checking.

topics.title: Combining sets: union, intersection and difference
topics.summary: Use |, &, - and ^ (and their method names) to combine sets, and test subsets and same-items-in-any-order.

knowledge_points.title: Union | : in either
knowledge_points.practice: Predict unions; write the union of two given sets.

knowledge_points.title: Intersection & : in both
knowledge_points.practice: Predict intersections; write code that finds common items of two lists via sets.

knowledge_points.title: Difference - and symmetric difference ^
knowledge_points.practice: Predict differences in both directions; choose the operator for described questions.

knowledge_points.title: Subsets and order-free equality
knowledge_points.practice: Predict subset and equality tests; write a check that a recipe's ingredients are all available.

topics.title: Lists of lists: grids
topics.summary: Read and change cells of a 2D list with grid[row][col], get its size, and loop over all cells with nested loops.

knowledge_points.title: Double indexing: row, then column
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3],
        [4, 5, 6]]
print(grid[1])     # [4, 5, 6]
print(grid[1][0])  # 4
grid[r] is a whole row (a list); grid[r][c] is one cell in it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict single and double indexing; write the expression for a described cell, including negative indexes.

knowledge_points.title: Changing a cell and measuring the grid
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
grid[0][2] = 7
print(grid)          # [[0, 0, 7], [0, 0, 0]]
print(len(grid), len(grid[0]))  # 2 3
len(grid) is the number of rows; len(grid[0]) the number of columns.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the grid after cell assignments; fix code that swaps row and column (IndexError).

knowledge_points.title: Nested for over rows and values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
total = 0
for row in grid:
    for value in row:
        total += value
print(total)  # 21
The outer loop hands you each row list; the inner loop walks along it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a grid total or count; predict how many times the inner body runs.

knowledge_points.title: Nested range loops when you need positions
knowledge_points.practice: Write a search returning the (row, col) of a value; reorder the nested index loop lines.

topics.title: Working with grid rows, columns and diagonals
topics.summary: Compute row sums, extract a column, walk a diagonal and transpose a grid, as in tic-tac-toe and sudoku checks.

knowledge_points.title: A row is a list: sum or check it directly
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
for row in grid:
    print(sum(row))
# 6
# 15
Built-ins that work on lists work on each row.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict row sums and maxima; write a check that every row has the same sum.

knowledge_points.title: A column needs one item from every row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
col = []
for row in grid:
    col.append(row[1])
print(col)  # [2, 5]
There is no grid[:][1]; collect row[c] from each row.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a column extractor; fix code that uses grid[1] when it meant column 1.

knowledge_points.title: Diagonals: the row and column index move together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
board = [['X', 'O', 'O'],
         ['O', 'X', 'O'],
         ['O', 'O', 'X']]
diag = []
for i in range(3):
    diag.append(board[i][i])
print(diag)  # ['X', 'X', 'X']
The main diagonal is board[i][i]; the other one is board[i][2 - i].
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the index for the anti-diagonal; write a tic-tac-toe win check for diagonals.

knowledge_points.title: Transposing: rows become columns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
flipped = []
for c in range(len(grid[0])):
    new_row = []
    for row in grid:
        new_row.append(row[c])
    flipped.append(new_row)
print(flipped)  # [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
Each column of the old grid becomes a row of the new one; a 2x3 grid becomes 3x2.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the transpose lines; predict the shape and contents of a transposed grid.

topics.title: Lists of dictionaries as records
topics.summary: Store records as a list of dicts, read fields inside a loop, filter records, find the best by a field, and add a new record.

knowledge_points.title: Index the list, then the key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = [{'name': 'Ana', 'age': 31},
          {'name': 'Bo', 'age': 27}]
print(people[1]['name'])  # Bo
people[1] is a dict; ['name'] then looks inside it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict two-step lookups; write the expression for a described field of a described record.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over records and read fields
knowledge_points.practice: Write a filter that prints matching names; fix a loop that writes people['age'] instead of p['age'].

knowledge_points.title: Best record by a field
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = [{'name': 'Ana', 'age': 31}, {'name': 'Bo', 'age': 27}]
oldest = people[0]
for p in people:
    if p['age'] > oldest['age']:
        oldest = p
print(oldest['name'])  # Ana
Keep the whole best record, not just its number, so you can report any field.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the youngest/highest-scoring search; predict output with a tie.

knowledge_points.title: Adding a record and missing fields
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = [{'name': 'Ana', 'age': 31}]
people.append({'name': 'Cy'})
for p in people:
    print(p['name'], p.get('age', '?'))
# Ana 31
# Cy ?
append a new dict; records may lack a field, so read optional fields with get.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code appending a record built from input values; fix a loop that crashes on a record missing a key.

topics.title: Dicts holding lists and dicts
topics.summary: Look up and update values inside a dict of lists (gradebook) and a dict of dicts (profiles), and loop over them.

knowledge_points.title: A dict of lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grades = {'ana': [90, 85], 'bo': [70]}
print(grades['ana'])     # [90, 85]
print(grades['ana'][1])  # 85
print(sum(grades['ana']) / len(grades['ana']))  # 87.5
The key picks a list; then index or use list built-ins on it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lookups and averages; write the average for a named student.

knowledge_points.title: Appending to an inner list
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict after appends; fix grades['bo'] = 88 that replaced the list.

knowledge_points.title: A dict of dicts
knowledge_points.practice: Predict nested lookups and updates; write the update for a described change.

knowledge_points.title: Looping over a dict of dicts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = {'ana': {'age': 31, 'city': 'Oslo'},
          'bo': {'age': 27, 'city': 'Lima'}}
for name, info in people.items():
    print(name, 'lives in', info['city'])
# ana lives in Oslo
# bo lives in Lima
items() gives each outer key with its inner dict; read fields from the inner dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the loop lines; write a loop that prints everyone over a given age.

topics.title: Finding your way through deeply nested data
topics.summary: Follow a path of keys and indexes through JSON-shaped data, loop over a list inside a dict, and tell from the error which step failed.

knowledge_points.title: Read a path one step at a time
knowledge_points.practice: Write the access path for a described value; trace the type after each step.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over the list you reach
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop printing a field from each item of a nested list; predict its output.

knowledge_points.title: Which step went wrong?
knowledge_points.practice: Match each failing path to its error; fix paths that skip a list level.

knowledge_points.title: Defaults at each level with get
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = {'meta': {'page': 2}}
print(data.get('meta', {}).get('page', 1))   # 2
print(data.get('extra', {}).get('page', 1))  # 1
A default of {} lets the next get run safely when an optional level is missing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict chained get results; rewrite a crashing path with get defaults.

topics.title: match on the shape of data: sequence and mapping patterns
topics.summary: Use case patterns that match lists by length and contents ([x, y], [first, *rest]) and dicts by keys ({'type': t}).

knowledge_points.title: Sequence patterns match length and items
knowledge_points.worked_example:
command = 'go north'.split()
match command:
    case ['go', direction]:
        print('going', direction)  # going north
    case ['quit']:
        print('bye')
A list pattern matches only a list of exactly that length; literals must be equal, names capture.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which case runs for several commands; write a case for a two-word command.

knowledge_points.title: A star collects the rest
knowledge_points.worked_example:
command = ['drop', 'key', 'map']
match command:
    case ['drop', *items]:
        print(items)  # ['key', 'map']
*name matches any number of items, including none, just like star unpacking.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the captured list (including empty); fix a pattern that fails because the length is fixed.

knowledge_points.title: Mapping patterns match keys
knowledge_points.worked_example:
event = {'type': 'click', 'x': 3, 'y': 4}
match event:
    case {'type': 'key', 'key': k}:
        print('key', k)
    case {'type': 'click', 'x': x, 'y': y}:
        print('click at', x, y)  # click at 3 4
A dict pattern needs the listed keys with matching values; extra keys in the data are allowed.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which case runs for several events; write a mapping pattern for a described event.

knowledge_points.title: Order of cases and the fallback
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for cmd in [['look'], ['go'], ['go', 'up', 'now']]:
    match cmd:
        case ['go', where]:
            print('go', where)
        case [verb]:
            print('just', verb)
        case _:
            print('unknown')
# just look
# just go
# unknown
Cases are tried top to bottom; ['go'] fails the 2-item pattern but matches [verb].
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs for a list of inputs; reorder cases so a specific pattern is not shadowed.

topics.title: List comprehensions: transforming every item
topics.summary: Replace a loop-and-append with [expression for item in iterable] to build a new list from each item.

knowledge_points.title: From loop-and-append to a comprehension
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
squares = []
for n in nums:
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)                # [1, 4, 9]
print([n * n for n in nums])  # [1, 4, 9]
The comprehension packs the loop and the append into one expression: what to keep, then the for.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite short append loops as comprehensions; fill in the expression part of a comprehension.

knowledge_points.title: Any expression, any iterable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['hi', 'there']
print([w.upper() for w in words])    # ['HI', 'THERE']
print([len(w) for w in words])       # [2, 5]
print([i * 10 for i in range(4)])    # [0, 10, 20, 30]
Method calls, functions and arithmetic all work; strings and ranges work as the source too.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict comprehension results over lists, strings and ranges.

knowledge_points.title: A comprehension builds a new list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
prices = [10, 20]
with_tax = [p * 1.5 for p in prices]
print(prices, with_tax)  # [10, 20] [15.0, 30.0]
The original list is untouched; assign the result to keep it.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that writes a comprehension but never assigns it; predict both lists afterwards.

knowledge_points.title: Parsing text into numbers in one line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = '3 14 15'
nums = [int(x) for x in line.split()]
print(nums, sum(nums))  # [3, 14, 15] 32
split gives strings; the comprehension converts each one.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the parse line for comma- or space-separated numbers; fix a version that sums strings.

topics.title: Filtering in a comprehension, and if-else inside one
topics.summary: Keep only matching items with a trailing if, combine filtering with a transform, and tell it apart from an if-else expression at the front.

knowledge_points.title: A trailing if keeps only matching items
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7, -3]
print([n for n in nums if n > 0])  # [4, 7]
Items whose condition is False are skipped; the result may be shorter.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict filtered lists; write a comprehension keeping even numbers.

knowledge_points.title: Filter and transform together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['a', 'tree', 'is', 'green']
print([w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 2])  # ['TREE', 'GREEN']
The if decides which items survive; the front expression decides what is stored for each survivor.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the parts of a comprehension (Parsons on tokens); write one from a described loop with if and append.

knowledge_points.title: if-else at the front changes values, keeps every item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7]
print(['pos' if n > 0 else 'neg' for n in nums])  # ['pos', 'neg', 'pos']
print([n if n > 0 else 0 for n in nums])          # [4, 0, 7]
A conditional expression before for picks a value for every item, so the length never changes.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results and their lengths; choose between front if-else and trailing if for described tasks.

knowledge_points.title: else at the end is a syntax error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7]
print([n for n in nums if n > 0 else 0])  # SyntaxError: invalid syntax
A trailing if cannot have else; move the if-else in front of for if every item should get a value.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix misplaced if-else comprehensions; predict which comprehensions are valid.

topics.title: Comprehensions with sum(), any() and all()
topics.summary: Feed comprehensions to sum/max/min, answer 'any?' and 'all?' questions with any() and all(), and know their empty-list results.

knowledge_points.title: Totals, maxima and counts in one line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['hi', 'there', 'you']
print(sum([len(w) for w in words]))   # 10
print(max([len(w) for w in words]))   # 5
print(sum([1 for w in words if 'h' in w]))  # 2
Build the list of numbers you want, then hand it to a built-in. Summing 1 for each match counts matches.
knowledge_points.practice: Write one-line totals and counts; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: any() and all() replace search flags
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7]
print(any([n < 0 for n in nums]))  # True
print(all([n < 0 for n in nums]))  # False
any is True if at least one value is True; all only if every one is. They replace the found = False loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a flag loop with any or all; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Empty lists: any is False, all is True
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(any([]))  # False
print(all([]))  # True
print(all([n > 0 for n in []]))  # True
'Every one of nothing' is vacuously true; guard with a length check if an empty input should fail.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict any/all on empty and filtered-to-empty lists; fix a validator that accepts an empty list.

topics.title: Comprehensions over grids: nested and two-for comprehensions
topics.summary: Pull a column or row totals from a grid, build a grid safely, flatten a grid and build pairs with two for clauses.

knowledge_points.title: One comprehension over the rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print([row[0] for row in grid])   # [1, 4]
print([sum(row) for row in grid])  # [6, 15]
Each item is a row, so the expression can index or sum it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write comprehensions for a column and for row maxima; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Building a grid with a comprehension
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
grid[0][0] = 1
print(grid)  # [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
Each pass makes a fresh row, so changing one cell does not change the others (unlike [[0] * 3] * 2).
knowledge_points.practice: Write a comprehension for an h-by-w grid of a given value; fix grid code built with * on the outer list.

knowledge_points.title: Two for clauses flatten a grid
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print([x for row in grid for x in row])  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
The for clauses read in the same order as nested loops: outer first, inner second.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the clauses to match a given nested loop; predict flattened results.

knowledge_points.title: Pairs from two loops, with a filter
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print([(a, b) for a in range(3) for b in range(3) if a < b])
# [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]
Every combination of a and b is tried; the if keeps the ones you want. Past two clauses, a plain loop is clearer.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the pairs produced; write a comprehension for all pairs with a given sum.

topics.title: Dictionary comprehensions: building a dict in one line
topics.summary: Write {key: value for item in iterable}, including from two lists with zip and with a filter, and predict what happens when keys repeat.

knowledge_points.title: Key and value from each item
knowledge_points.practice: Predict dict comprehensions; rewrite an empty-dict-and-assign loop as one.

knowledge_points.title: Keys and values from two lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['ana', 'bo']
ages = [31, 27]
print({n: a for n, a in zip(names, ages)})  # {'ana': 31, 'bo': 27}
Unpack each zipped pair; the comprehension can then transform either side (dict(zip()) cannot).
knowledge_points.practice: Write a comprehension mapping names to upper-case names or doubled values; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Filtering with a trailing if
knowledge_points.practice: Predict filtered dict comprehensions; fill in the condition for a described filter.

knowledge_points.title: Repeated keys: the last one wins
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results with repeated keys; choose between a dict comprehension and grouping for described tasks.

topics.title: Transforming and filtering dicts, and set comprehensions
topics.summary: Build a new dict from an existing one's items (change values, filter by value, swap keys and values) and write set comprehensions.

knowledge_points.title: Changing every value
knowledge_points.practice: Write a comprehension applying a discount; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Keeping entries that pass a test
knowledge_points.practice: Write a filter by value or by key; fix a loop that deletes entries while iterating by rewriting it as a comprehension.

knowledge_points.title: Swapping keys and values
knowledge_points.practice: Predict inversions with unique and repeated values; choose comprehension or grouping.

knowledge_points.title: Set comprehensions: braces without a colon
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['Hi', 'hi', 'Yo']
print(sorted({w.lower() for w in words}))  # ['hi', 'yo']
print(type({w: 1 for w in words}))  # <class 'dict'>
{expr for ...} builds a set (duplicates dropped); {k: v for ...} builds a dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each comprehension makes a set, dict or list and its contents; write a set comprehension of distinct first letters.

topics.title: Stacks: last in, first out with a list
topics.summary: Use a list as a stack with append() and pop(), peek and test for empty safely, and solve bracket matching with a stack.

knowledge_points.title: Push with append, pop from the end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
stack = []
stack.append('a')
stack.append('b')
stack.append('c')
print(stack.pop())  # c
print(stack)        # ['a', 'b']
The last item pushed is the first popped (LIFO), like a stack of plates.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict pop results after a sequence of pushes and pops; trace the stack contents.

knowledge_points.title: Peek and check for empty before popping
knowledge_points.worked_example:
stack = ['a']
print(stack[-1])  # a  (peek, nothing removed)
stack.pop()
if stack:
    print('more')
else:
    print('empty')  # empty
stack.pop()  # IndexError: pop from empty list
stack[-1] looks without removing; test with if stack: before popping.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that pops an empty stack; predict outputs with peek vs pop.

knowledge_points.title: Undo: popping reverses the order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
history = []
for action in ['type', 'bold', 'delete']:
    history.append(action)
while history:
    print('undo', history.pop())
# undo delete
# undo bold
# undo type
Popping everything gives the items back newest first: the basis of undo and reversing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict an undo sequence; write a function reversing a string with a stack.

knowledge_points.title: Matching brackets with a stack
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the stack on a given string; fix a version that forgets the final empty check.

topics.title: Queues: first in, first out with deque
topics.summary: Model a FIFO queue, see why list.pop(0) is the slow way, and use collections.deque with append(), popleft() and maxlen.

knowledge_points.title: FIFO: serve in arrival order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = ['ana', 'bo']
line.append('cy')
print(line.pop(0))  # ana
print(line)         # ['bo', 'cy']
Join at the back, leave from the front. pop(0) works, but every remaining item shifts down one place.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict who is served after a sequence of joins and serves; multiple choice on stack vs queue for described situations.

knowledge_points.title: deque: a queue built for both ends
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import deque
q = deque(['ana', 'bo'])
q.append('cy')
print(q.popleft())  # ana
print(q)            # deque(['bo', 'cy'])
popleft() removes from the front without shifting, so it stays fast for long queues. Copy the import line as given.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a list queue using deque; predict q after mixed append/popleft.

knowledge_points.title: Process until the queue is empty
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import deque
jobs = deque(['print', 'save'])
while jobs:
    job = jobs.popleft()
    print('doing', job)
    if job == 'print':
        jobs.append('log')
# doing print
# doing save
# doing log
while jobs: stops when nothing is left; new work added during the loop joins the back.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the queue through a processing loop; predict the order of work.

knowledge_points.title: appendleft and maxlen: keep only the latest
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import deque
recent = deque(maxlen=3)
for page in ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']:
    recent.append(page)
print(list(recent))  # ['b', 'c', 'd']
recent.appendleft('z')
print(list(recent))  # ['z', 'b', 'c']
With maxlen, adding to a full deque drops an item from the other end.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict contents of a bounded deque; write a 'last 5 entries' history.

topics.title: Counting with collections.Counter
topics.summary: Count items with Counter, read counts (missing is 0), get the most common with most_common(), and add more counts.

knowledge_points.title: Counter counts any iterable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter('banana')
print(c['a'], c['n'], c['z'])  # 3 2 0
One call replaces the counting loop; a missing key reads as 0 instead of raising KeyError.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts including missing keys; rewrite a get(k, 0) counting loop with Counter.

knowledge_points.title: most_common(n) for the top n
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
words = 'the cat and the hat and the bat'.split()
print(Counter(words).most_common(2))  # [('the', 3), ('and', 2)]
Returns (item, count) pairs, biggest first: the sort-by-value work done for you.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict most_common results; write a top-3 report with unpacking.

knowledge_points.title: Adding more counts with update() and +
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter(['a', 'b'])
c.update(['a', 'c'])
print(c['a'])  # 2
print((Counter('ab') + Counter('bc'))['b'])  # 2
update adds counts (unlike dict.update, which replaces values); + combines two Counters.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts after update and +; multiple choice contrasting Counter.update with dict.update.

knowledge_points.title: A Counter is still a dict
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter('aab')
for ch, n in c.items():
    print(ch, n)
# a 2
# b 1
print(len(c), 'a' in c, 'z' in c)  # 2 True False
Loops, len and in work as on a dict; reading c['z'] gives 0 but does not add 'z'.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict loops and membership on a Counter; fix code that expects c['z'] to raise KeyError.

topics.title: Automatic defaults with collections.defaultdict
topics.summary: Count with defaultdict(int) and group with defaultdict(list), and know that reading a missing key creates it.

knowledge_points.title: defaultdict(int) for counting
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a get(k, 0) counter with defaultdict; predict the counts.

knowledge_points.title: defaultdict(list) for grouping
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a setdefault grouping loop; predict the groups.

knowledge_points.title: Pass the type, don't call it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import defaultdict
ok = defaultdict(list)
bad = defaultdict(list())  # TypeError: first argument must be callable or None
defaultdict needs something it can call later to make each default: list, int, set, not list().
knowledge_points.practice: Fix broken defaultdict constructions; choose int, list or set for described tasks.

knowledge_points.title: Reading a missing key adds it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import defaultdict
d = defaultdict(int)
print(d['x'])     # 0
print(dict(d))    # {'x': 0}
print('y' in d)   # False
Unlike get, looking up creates the entry; test with in when you only want to check.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict after lookups; fix a check that accidentally adds keys.

topics.title: Records with named fields: namedtuple
topics.summary: Define a namedtuple type, read fields by name, use it like a tuple, and make changed copies with _replace().

knowledge_points.title: Define a record type and read fields by name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(3, 4)
print(p.x, p.y)  # 3 4
print(p)         # Point(x=3, y=4)
p.x reads better than p[0] and prints with its field names.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict field access and printing; write a namedtuple definition for a described record.

knowledge_points.title: Still a tuple: index, unpack, compare, cannot change
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(3, 4)
x, y = p
print(p[0], x, p == (3, 4))  # 3 3 True
p.x = 5  # AttributeError: can't set attribute
Everything a tuple does still works; fields are read-only.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict tuple operations on a namedtuple; fix code that assigns to a field.

knowledge_points.title: A list of named records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Pet = namedtuple('Pet', ['name', 'age'])
pets = [Pet('Rex', 3), Pet('Tom', 5)]
for pet in pets:
    if pet.age > 4:
        print(pet.name)  # Tom
Replaces lists of plain tuples where you had to remember which position meant what.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite an index-based loop over tuples with field names; predict outputs.

knowledge_points.title: Keyword creation and _replace()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(x=1, y=2)
q = p._replace(y=9)
print(p, q)  # Point(x=1, y=2) Point(x=1, y=9)
_replace returns a new record with some fields changed; the original stays the same.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both records after _replace; write code moving a point one step right.

topics.title: Every combination: product, combinations and permutations
topics.summary: Replace nested loops with itertools.product, and list unordered pairs with combinations and ordered arrangements with permutations.

knowledge_points.title: product() replaces nested loops
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import product
print(list(product([1, 2], 'ab')))
# [(1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
Same tuples, same order as a loop over 1, 2 with an inner loop over 'a', 'b'. list() shows the results.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a two-level nested loop with product; predict the tuples.

knowledge_points.title: combinations(): unordered picks, no repeats
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import combinations
for a, b in combinations(['ana', 'bo', 'cy'], 2):
    print(a, 'vs', b)
# ana vs bo
# ana vs cy
# bo vs cy
Each pair appears once, like a loop where the inner index starts after the outer one.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict pairs; write a schedule of matches for a list of players.

knowledge_points.title: permutations(): order matters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import permutations
print(list(permutations('abc', 2)))
# [('a', 'b'), ('a', 'c'), ('b', 'a'), ('b', 'c'), ('c', 'a'), ('c', 'b')]
('a', 'b') and ('b', 'a') are different arrangements, so there are twice as many as combinations.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict permutations of short inputs; count them with len(list(...)).

knowledge_points.title: Which tool for which question?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import combinations, permutations, product
print(len(list(product('HT', repeat=3))))     # 8
print(len(list(combinations(range(5), 2))))  # 10
print(len(list(permutations(range(5), 2))))  # 20
Repeats allowed: product. Choose a group: combinations. Order a line-up: permutations.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the right function for word problems and give the count.

topics.title: Joining and stretching iterables: chain, count and zip_longest
topics.summary: Loop over several lists in a row with chain, number things endlessly with count, and handle lists of different lengths with zip_longest or zip(strict=True).

knowledge_points.title: chain(): one loop over several lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import chain
total = 0
for x in chain([1, 2], [3, 4]):
    total += x
print(total)  # 10
print(list(chain([1, 2], 'ab')))  # [1, 2, 'a', 'b']
No new combined list is built; items come from each input in turn.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict chained output; rewrite two loops over two lists as one loop with chain.

knowledge_points.title: count(): an endless counter
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import count
for n in count(10, 5):
    if n > 25:
        break
    print(n)
# 10
# 15
# 20
# 25
count never stops by itself; pair it with break (or zip) to end the loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output; fix a count loop that never ends.

knowledge_points.title: zip stops early; zip_longest fills the gaps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import zip_longest
names = ['ana', 'bo', 'cy']
scores = [90, 80]
print(list(zip(names, scores)))  # [('ana', 90), ('bo', 80)]
print(list(zip_longest(names, scores, fillvalue=0)))
# [('ana', 90), ('bo', 80), ('cy', 0)]
Plain zip silently drops the extra item; zip_longest keeps it and pads with fillvalue (None by default).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both results for uneven lists; choose which to use.

knowledge_points.title: zip(strict=True) refuses uneven lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['ana', 'bo', 'cy']
scores = [90, 80]
print(list(zip(names, scores, strict=True)))
# ValueError: zip() argument 2 is shorter than argument 1
When lengths should match, strict=True turns a silent bug into an error.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise ValueError; fix code that silently lost data.
